name: splats
description: A small, hand-made collection of objects as 3D Gaussian splats: everyday things scanned from phone video, classic meshes converted directly from geometry, and a few generated by an AI model from a single image. Each one is labelled with how it was made and what license it carries.
license: per object (see each record's license field)
license_note: The collection has no single license. Scanned objects are CC-BY-4.0 (credit Marcel Padilla); objects derived from a mesh inherit that mesh's license (CC0, public domain, or Stanford 3DSR research-use with attribution); generated objects are as-is with no warranty of rights. Every record carries its own license, license_url and license_open flag.

citation.text: Marcel Padilla. splats: a small collection of Gaussian splat objects. 2026. https://github.com/marcelpadilla/splats

objects.author: Marcel Padilla
objects.attribution: Generated from 'Chair.JPG' by Antonio Borrillo, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons. A bentwood cafe chair. Furniture is the one category here where the object can carry its own copyright as applied art (in the EU, life + 70 since Cofemel, C-683/17), so this batch uses only the vernacular bentwood type, whose form dates to Michael Thonet's No. 14 of 1859; Thonet died in 1871. A named 20th-century designer chair was found and rejected for exactly this reason.

objects.author: Marcel Padilla
objects.attribution: Generated from 'Early Android phone by EMOBILE.jpg' by Syced, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons. A mobile handset is a useful article, so it carries no copyright as a sculptural work. Two further questions were checked for this one. Its SCREEN IS OFF, so no copyrighted user interface is reproduced in the object. And its shape carries no visible maker's mark: a recent flagship's appearance can still be covered by a registered design right, which runs up to 25 years, so an unbranded early handset was chosen rather than a current model.
